2. The respondents instituted Title Suit No. 57 of 1999 in the 1st Court of the learned Joint District Judge, Narayanganj for declaration of title and recovery of khas pogsession contending, inter alia, that "Ka" schedule property appertaining to C.S. Plot No. 78 comprising an area of 151 decimals of land fell in the saham of Kalai and Ahmed, and other co-sharers got other lands. Thereafter by an amicable partition between them Kalai got a share of 90 decimals of land and Ahmed got the rest 69 decimals out of 1.50 acres of land. During C.S. operation Kalai and Ahmed being found in possession their names were duly recorded to the extent of 1.59 acres of land. As they failed to pay rents, the landlord Ashutosh Banerjee got a decree for arrears of rent in Rent Suit No. 2526 of 1929 in the 4th Court of Munsif, Narayaranganj, and in pursuance of Rent Execution Case No. 45 of 1933 the landlord purchased 90 decimals of land. The sale certificate was registered through Court in favour of Ashutosh Benerjee on 17th July, 1933, and thereafter the landlord auction purchaser settled 80 decimals of land from the east- cm side in favour of one Kamar Ali and while he was owning and possessing the same, he transfeged 40 decimals of land to Rekmat Ali by registered deed No. 2513 dated 25th February, 1948 and thereafter Kamar Ali also transferred 40 decimals of land to Rekmat Ali and accordingly Rekmat Ali became owner in possession of entire 80 decimals of land. Ramat Ali died leaving behind his wife Golbahar Bibi, four sons namely, Monsur Ali, Montazuddin, Sukkur Ali and. Jainuddin and one daughter Asi Khatun. The Munsur Ali got 40 decimals of land from southern side and Momtazuddin got 40 decimals out of 80 decimals from their father Rekmat Ali by amicable family arrangement. Momtazuddin transferred his entire 40 decimals of land to his daughter Batashi by registered deed dated 11th October, 1966(Ext. 5). The R.S. Khatian No. 1630 has been prepared in her name for this 40 decimals of land and R.S. Khatian No. 1854 (l3xt.9) has been prepared in the name of MunSur Ali in respect of 37 decimals but in fact he had 40 decimals of land out of which 30 decimals had been acquired by the government in L. A. Case No. 140 of 1962-60 and while owning and possessing the remaining 10 decimals of land, Munsur All died leaving the plaintiffs as his heirs  and then they were dispossessed by the defendants on 7th April, 1999. 

 3. The defendants petitioners contested the suit denying the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia, that 1.59 acres of land of suit plot belonged to Kalai and Ahmed and both of them got 7912 decimals of land each, that Nabalakshmi Debya and others were the actual owners of the suit khatian and that C.S. recorded tenant. Kalai died leaving-I hind -two sons namely, Charag Ali and Rekmot Ali. Charage All got the eastern portion of the land to the extent of 3912 decimals and Rekmot Ali got 3912 decimals of land towards the western side and on his death, his two daughters i.e. the defendant-petitioner No. 1 of Title Suit No. 57 of 1999 and the plaintiff-respondent Nos. 1 and 2 of Title Suit No. 84 of 1999 and his wife Anwara Begum alias Tamaji Begum inherited his sham Anwara Begiim also died leaving behind the said two daughters who got the said land in question. 

 5. Mr. Syed Amirul Islam, the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioners submitted that the High Court Division erred in law in failing to consider that the Court of appeal below on consideration of the certified copy of the C.S. Khatian exhibited by the plaintiffs and the corresponding original C.S. Khatian filed by the defendants held that the C.S. Khatians did not indicate that Ashutosh Banarjee held superior interest in the suit land and disbelieved Kalai's acquisition of title and these being findings of fact are immune from interference by the High Court Division exercising the revisional jurisdiction in the absence of any misreading or non-consideration of the evidence on record in arriving at such findings. Learned Counsel further contended that the Court of appeal below having held that exts. 3(a) and 3(g) did not attract the suit land, there is no legal evidence to substantiate the plaintiffs claim of acquisition of title in the suit land and that the plaintiffs having failed to prove their claim of possession followed by dispossession by the defendants, the learned Judges of the High Court Division fell in an error in interfering with those findings of facts and restoring those of the trial Court.
